source_metadata.title: The Bitter Lesson of Tool Calling
source_metadata.organization: Commercial Technology and Innovation Office, PricewaterhouseCoopers, U.S.A

atoms.canonical_statement: The study evaluates whether programmatic tool calling can replace native JSON tool calling without sacrificing tool-calling accuracy, including under chaining, parallel fan-out, and context-rot conditions.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: we empirically compare programmatic tool calling (PTC) to native JSON tool calling across 14 language models on BFCL v4

atoms.canonical_statement: In the programmatic tool-calling condition, models receive typed Python stubs corresponding one-to-one with function schemas, write a Python script that calls the stubs, and have the script executed in a native shell subprocess.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The model writes a Python script that imports this module and calls the appropriate functions.

atoms.canonical_statement: In the JSON tool-calling reference condition, function schemas are provided as JSON tool definitions and the model emits structured JSON tool-call objects through the tool-calling API.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The model outputs a structured JSON object at each function call.

atoms.canonical_statement: An entry is scored correct only when the produced set of function calls matches the ground-truth calls after normalized string comparison that strips punctuation and lowercases values.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: matches C* under the benchmark’s normalized string comparison, which strips punctuation and lowercases all values before matching

outcome.definition: All required function calls and arguments match ground truth after normalized string comparison.

atoms.canonical_statement: The main evaluation uses a representative 309-entry BFCL v4 subset spanning eight task categories, sampled proportionally to mirror the full benchmark with per-category minimums for smaller categories.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: 309 representative entries drawn from eight task categories

population.label: Representative BFCL v4 subset spanning eight task categories

atoms.canonical_statement: The deterministic scorer reports the fraction of entries for which every required function call is present and correctly parameterized; syntax or runtime errors in the PTC subprocess score zero correct calls, and no entries are skipped.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: When the shell subprocess raises a syntax or runtime error, the entry is scored as zero correct calls. No entries are skipped or excluded

atoms.canonical_statement: The chaining ablation contains 52 entries with chain lengths from 2 to 20, weighted toward longer chains; 17 entries have chain length at least 6 and 10 have chain length at least 13.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The chaining subset (n = 52) was optimized to cover the full range of chain lengths (nchain = 2–20)

population.label: Chaining ablation entries with chain lengths 2–20

atoms.canonical_statement: The parallelism ablation reports 32 enumeration-type entries with fan-out counts of 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 20, 30, and 48, and adds Claude Sonnet 5 probes at N=60, 70, 72, 75, and 100.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The parallelism subset (n = 32) covers fan-out counts of 7 to 48 (7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 20, 30, 48)

population.label: Parallelism enumeration-type ablation entries

atoms.canonical_statement: The context-rot ablation compares a filtered condition containing only relevant function schemas with a flood condition containing 128 total schemas, including relevant functions plus unrelated decoys; each condition contains 31 entries.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: flood (128 total schemas, including the relevant functions plus corpus decoys drawn from unrelated domains)

population.label: Context-rot ablation entries per condition

atoms.canonical_statement: The evaluation covers 14 language models from Anthropic and OpenAI released across approximately 20 months, and all models are run at temperature 0.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We evaluate 14 models spanning two families and 20 months of releases

population.label: Language models from Anthropic and OpenAI

atoms.canonical_statement: Results use 95% Wilson confidence intervals; because ablation samples are small, individual-model ablation results are treated as directional, pairwise comparisons are not corrected for multiple testing, and no individual-model significance claim is made.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Pairwise per-model comparisons are not corrected for multiple testing. We make no claim that any individual model result is statistically significant in isolation.

atoms.canonical_statement: In aggregation tasks, some models produced correct aggregate answers from parametric world knowledge without executing all enumeration calls; the authors therefore treat enumeration accuracy as the primary measure of tool-execution fidelity.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Several models produce the correct aggregation answer by drawing on parametric world knowledge rather than executing the enumeration calls.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors conclude that programmatic tool calling is a viable and reliable alternative to JSON tool calling, with relative performance tracking model generation and with advantages in high fan-out and context-rot settings.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: These results demonstrate that programmatic tool calling is a viable and reliable alternative to JSON tool calling

atoms.canonical_statement: BFCL v4 in this evaluation uses echo-return stubs that return their arguments instead of executing real APIs, so the study measures argument-serialization accuracy rather than end-to-end tool-use correctness and may not generalize to chains that depend on actual return values.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: BFCL v4 uses echo-return stubs. Each function returns its arguments verbatim rather than executing real API calls.

atoms.canonical_statement: The ablation conditions contain only 31 to 52 entries, producing wide confidence intervals; the authors state that individual-model results should be interpreted as directional and reserve stronger interpretation for aggregate cross-model patterns.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: the ablation entry counts are small (n = 31–52 per condition), so individual model results carry wide confidence intervals and should be read as directional

atoms.canonical_statement: Although the deterministic scorer avoids BFCL v4’s LLM-judge path, the evaluation may still inherit noise from benchmark ground-truth labels.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: the benchmark’s ground-truth labels may still contain noise that our scorer inherits.

atoms.canonical_statement: PTC has fixed input-token overhead because its instruction template is embedded as prose; on the chaining ablation it used 1.5 times the input tokens of JSON tool calling, although this overhead reversed at high fan-out, and output-token counts did not differ across paradigms.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: On the chaining ablation, programmatic tool calling uses 1.5× the input tokens of JSON tool calling. This overhead reverses at high fan-out

extraction_limitations: Atoms were extracted from the uploaded 11-page arXiv preprint; no external verification was performed because @VERIFY was not activated.
No funding disclosure or conflict-of-interest statement was found in the accessible main-text PDF, so no funding_disclosure or conflict_of_interest atoms were created.

The paper states that evaluation entry ID lists are released with an evaluation harness, but the PDF does not provide a repository URL in the extracted text; the data_availability atom therefore records only what is stated.

Latency results reported as a range (0.32–0.96 of baseline across 13 models) were preserved in a qualitative_result atom because the current QuantitativeResult schema requires a single central estimate.
Figure 1 and Figure 2 were visually inspected; atoms were not duplicated when the same assertion was already represented by the corresponding methods/results text or table.

The source contains internal numerical/wording inconsistencies: the abstract and Table 2 support a 10.6-percentage-point GPT-5.6 improvement while the conclusion says 10.7%, and Section 5.1 says all five Anthropic models match or exceed baseline across all three ablations despite Table 3 showing lower PTC chaining accuracy for Claude Haiku 4.5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5. Atoms use the directly tabulated values and avoid propagating the inconsistent broader claim.
All extracted atoms are marked needs_review; validation establishes structural and atom-kind sufficiency, not factual verification against independent sources.
